title: Origin of amniotes
summary: Amniotes, the group that includes reptiles, birds and mammals, lay a special kind of egg. A 2025 study of the earliest amniote tracks finds that dates for the group's origin cluster around a median of 319 million years ago, with a spread from 308.5 to 334.7 million. At Joggins in Nova Scotia, Hylonomus lyelli is described as the first true reptile.

uncertainty.note: Ages span the late Carboniferous (Bashkirian to Moscovian) cluster for crown-group amniotes centered around 319 Ma and the Joggins Formation yielding Hylonomus (c. 318–310 Ma).

as_recorded.value: spread of the cluster is 308.5 to 334.7 million years

where.modern_name: Joggins Fossil Cliffs, Nova Scotia, Canada (key fossil site)
where.historical_name: Equatorial coal swamps of Euramerica, late Carboniferous (Pennsylvanian); no polities existed

importance.justification: The evolution of the cleidoic amniotic egg decoupled vertebrate reproduction from water, enabling permanent colonization of dry land and giving rise to reptiles, dinosaurs, birds, and mammals.

related.because: The initial tetrapod colonization of land established the terrestrial vertebrate lineages that later evolved the amniotic egg.
Synapsid amniotes that diverged shortly after amniote origins diversified into the cynodont ancestors of mammals.
